opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think "resistance" is a real thing, but it's worth unpacking where it comes from.

In the Bay Area right now there's a very strong belief, almost an ideology, that the path forward is already known. You scale up data, scale up compute, keep refining the recipe, and capabilities keep improving. If you really believe that, then academic research looks a bit irrelevant. A professor with a few dozen GPUs can't train a frontier model, so why should anyone care what academia is doing? Some people say it quite openly: "academia should just stop doing this kind of work," or "everything interesting is happening inside the labs."

I understand that view. Industry has made enormous progress, and the engineering is genuinely hard and impressive. But I think it mixes up two things: making the current paradigm work really well, and figuring out what the next paradigm should be. Those are different jobs.

Industry is extremely good at the first. Once a direction is clear, a big lab can push it further than anyone else. But that same structure makes it hard to explore things that look unpromising at first, things that could take years, or ideas that go against the company's current roadmap. When you have a product, a valuation, and a race with competitors, you optimize for what you're confident will pay off in the next six to twelve months.

Academia is supposed to be the place where you can be wrong, where you can ask "what if the current approach is missing something fundamental?" Take vision and world models. A lot of current systems are built on language as the core, with vision attached. I think there are real questions about whether that's right: how a system should learn from the physical world, how representation learning should work, what intelligence even means beyond predicting the next token. Those questions don't have obvious scaling recipes yet, so they're exactly the kind of thing academia should work on.

There's also a cultural side. The Bay Area moves fast, and there's social pressure. If you're not at a frontier lab, people sometimes assume you're not doing important work. That can discourage students and push talent into a monoculture where everyone works on the same thing in the same way. Historically that's dangerous for a field. Deep learning itself came from people working on something the mainstream thought was a dead end.

So I don't see it as academia versus industry. They need each other. But the resistance mostly reflects a confidence that we already know the answer. I'm less sure we do, and that uncertainty is exactly why academic research still matters.

r001.rationale: It says the belief that scaling is the known path makes academic research seem irrelevant, including the view that a professor with few GPUs cannot train a frontier model.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss companies’ publication practices or how they affect outsiders’ view of their work.

r003.rationale: It does not describe a divide between research and product departments within an AI company.

r004.rationale: It mentions competitive pressure and near-term payoffs, but does not characterize staying at the forefront of the AI race as the sole goal of core model training departments.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "resistance" might be a slightly strong word, but I understand where the feeling comes from. When I was at Facebook AI Research and later moved to NYU, I felt this tension very directly. In the Bay Area right now, the center of gravity is clearly in industry labs. The compute is there, the data is there, and frankly a lot of the best people are there. So when you come from a university and talk about a paper, there's sometimes a reaction like, "That's nice, but does it scale? Did you run it on a real system?" There's an implicit assumption that if you didn't train the biggest model, you don't really know what's going on.

Part of that is legitimate. There are things you genuinely only learn at scale, and academics who pretend otherwise are fooling themselves. I take that seriously, which is one reason I try to keep my lab honest about what we can and cannot test.

But I think the skepticism also comes from a particular culture. Industry research now is very product-driven and very secretive. Papers are fewer, details are withheld, and success is measured by benchmark numbers or by shipping. In that environment, the slower, more exploratory style of academic work can look inefficient or even naive. People ask, why are you studying a small architecture question when the frontier has moved on?

My answer is that the frontier moves on because somebody asked those questions earlier. ResNeXt, the work on vision transformers, diffusion transformers, representation alignment, a lot of that started as fairly simple curiosity-driven experiments. Academia is where you can afford to be wrong in public, to publish negative results, to try something that does not obviously lead to a product. Industry has largely stopped doing that, and I think in the long run it will hurt them.

So I don't take the resistance personally. I see it as a sign of how fast the field has concentrated. What worries me more is that students start to believe it, and think the only real research happens behind a corporate wall. I want to show them that with a few GPUs, good taste, and the right questions, you can still change how people think about the problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes the view that academic work can seem inefficient or naive because it does not train the biggest models, and says students may believe only corporate research is real.

r002.rationale: It says industry research is secretive, papers are fewer, and details are withheld, communicating why outsiders cannot see much of companies’ work.

r003.rationale: It contrasts industry’s product-driven culture with academic work, but does not describe a divide between research and product departments within the same company.

r004.rationale: It mentions benchmark numbers, shipping, and the frontier, but does not say core model training departments have staying competitive as their sole goal.

astra-6.text:
我觉得这种抵触，首先要区分一下：大家抵触的是研究本身，还是学术界做研究的一套方式？这两个事情不完全一样。

在工业界，你每天面对很直接的反馈：模型有没有变好，用户愿不愿意用，成本能不能降下来。从这个角度看，有些学术工作为了发表论文，把一个问题包装得很复杂，但最后不一定解决实际问题。对这种现象的不满，我觉得可以理解，学术界也应该反思。

但如果因此觉得学术研究没有价值，我觉得又走到了另一个极端。不是所有值得研究的问题，都能用下一次产品发布的结果来衡量。有些工作最开始只是想弄清楚一个现象，甚至会得到一个负面的结果。它短期内可能没有用，但能让我们知道哪些假设是错的，哪些方向值得继续走。

所以我更关心的是，我们有没有保留提出不同问题的空间。如果所有人都用同一个指标、同一个时间尺度来判断价值，那看起来大家都很高效，但也可能只是越来越擅长做已经知道该怎么做的事情。学术界当然不能把“不需要立刻有用”当成逃避检验的理由；工业界也不应该把“现在用不上”等同于“不值得研究”。

r001.rationale: The response says some academic work may not solve practical problems and treats dissatisfaction with that lack of practical impact as understandable.

r002.rationale: It does not mention companies’ publication practices or outsiders being unable to see their work.

r003.rationale: It contrasts industry and academic priorities but does not describe a divide between research and product departments within one company.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss core model training departments or the competitive AI race as their sole goal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should first distinguish between resistance to academic research and frustration with how research is evaluated. Those are different things. You can criticize a system that rewards publication counts or small benchmark improvements without concluding that academic research itself has little value.

In industry, the feedback is very concrete: Does this improve the model? Does it make the product more useful? Can we deliver it quickly? That pressure is productive, but it can also make work with an uncertain payoff look wasteful. Academic research needs some room for questions whose importance is not obvious yet.

At the same time, academia has to take the criticism seriously. If the motivation for a project is mainly that it fits the next conference deadline, people will reasonably ask what we actually learned.

For me, the useful distinction is between research that creates understanding and research that merely produces an artifact. That applies equally to a university paper and an industry model release. We should ask: What new idea did this establish? What can other people build on? And would we still consider it valuable after the immediate excitement has passed?

r001.rationale: The response says criticism of evaluation should not be taken to mean academic research has little value; it does not identify belief in low impact as a basis for resistance.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss companies’ publication practices or outsiders’ ability to see their work.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe a divide between research and product departments within an AI company.

r004.rationale: The response mentions product usefulness and delivery pressure, but does not say core model training departments have staying ahead in the AI race as their sole goal.
